quickStart.keyIdea: Terraform is an infrastructure-as-code tool for declaring and managing the infrastructure resources an environment should contain.
quickStart.quickSummary:
Ansible mainly carries out configuration steps on existing machines, while Terraform defines the infrastructure that should exist and changes it to match. You describe networks, servers, databases, or services in configuration, and Terraform connects to platforms through providers to create, update, or remove them.

Terraform previews proposed changes with a plan before applying them and records managed resources in state, helping identify what differs from the desired setup. The comparison breaks down because Ansible can also create resources and Terraform can manage local objects; their primary focuses are different.

pages.title: 01 - Terraform’s Purpose and Core Model
02 - Configuration, Providers, and the Terraform Workflow
03 - State, Reconciliation, Modules, and Safe Operations
pages.rawNotes:
Terraform’s reconciliation model depends on state, which records mappings between configuration resources and real remote objects. During planning, Terraform uses state to compare what your configuration says should exist with what it previously observed and what the provider reports now. This is why Terraform can show additions, changes, and destructions as a calculated outcome rather than blindly running steps.

In basic usage, Terraform stores state in a local state file, which is convenient for experiments. In teams, a remote backend is commonly used so state is centralized and can support shared access, locking, and other backend features depending on the backend. Because state may contain sensitive values, you should treat it like confidential data by applying access control, encryption, and backup practices. Also note that terraform refresh is not typically a standalone workflow requirement, since modern planning and apply operations refresh provider data as needed.

Terraform modules help you organize and reuse configuration by packaging related resources into a reusable collection that accepts inputs and exposes outputs. A provider may update a resource in place when changed arguments are supported, but it can require replacement when changed arguments cannot be updated in place by the provider. Manual changes made outside Terraform can create drift, and a later plan may propose updates or replacements based on the mismatch between configuration, state, and current provider data. Provider behavior and state quality influence how Terraform interprets and reconciles those differences.

For safe operations, you should use code review, protect state, and follow least-privilege credentials so Terraform can do only what it needs. When refactoring, changing a resource address can be handled with a moved block to preserve identity and reduce unnecessary churn. Finally, treat destructive plans cautiously by reviewing them carefully before applying, since Terraform does not automatically and safely reconcile every manual change in every situation.

bridgeBlocks.body: Terraform and Ansible both use declarative-looking files to automate infrastructure, but they act at different layers. quickStart.keyIdea: Vue is a progressive framework for building interactive web interfaces from reusable pieces that stay synchronized with changing application data as an application grows from a small enhancement to a complete product.
quickStart.quickSummary:
Like React, Vue is a component-based JavaScript framework for building interactive user interfaces from reusable pieces and changing application state. Its reactive rendering model keeps the page aligned with state, so developers describe the interface instead of manually updating the DOM.

Vue differs from React mainly through its HTML-oriented templates, built-in directives, and more integrated official tools, while both support routing, shared state, and server-rendered applications. The comparison breaks at their boundaries: React is commonly treated as a UI library, whereas Vue provides a broader framework with clearer defaults and conventions.

pages.title: 01 - Vue’s Purpose and Core Model
pages.rawNotes:
## Vue’s purpose in one sentence
Vue is an open-source JavaScript framework for building user interfaces, created by Evan You and maintained by the Vue core team and community. Vue is designed for progressive adoption, so you can start by enhancing a small part of an existing HTML page or move all the way to building a full application.

## Progressive adoption: start small, scale up
A key idea behind Vue is that it does not force a single “all-or-nothing” approach. You can begin by using Vue to make one section of a page interactive, and later expand to a complete single-page application when your needs grow. This flexibility helps teams adopt Vue incrementally instead of rewriting everything at once.

## The core model: reactive rendering
Vue’s central model is reactive rendering, which connects application state to what the user sees. You declare state, write templates that describe the desired interface, and Vue coordinates updates when tracked state changes. When reactive data changes, Vue updates the affected rendered output, which reduces the need to manually manipulate the DOM.

## Components and templates: how the UI is organized
Vue uses components as the primary units of interface structure and reuse, so you can break an interface into smaller, independently organized pieces. Vue templates use HTML-based syntax with Vue-specific directives and expressions, which keeps your markup readable while still enabling dynamic behavior. Common directives include v-if, v-for, and v-bind.

## Vue 3 and reactivity under the hood
Vue 3 is the current major version and uses a modern reactivity system based on JavaScript Proxies. Vue can be used with plain JavaScript or TypeScript, and it supports both the Options API and the Composition API for organizing component logic.

## Minimal reactive counter example
Here is a minimal Vue 3 Single-File Component that shows a reactive counter, a template, and a click handler.

```vue
<template>
  <button @click="count++">Count: {{ count }}</button>
</template>

<script>
import { ref } from 'vue'

export default {
  setup() {
    const count = ref(0)
    return { count }
  }
}
</script>
```

## Vue vs “just rendering”
Vue is a framework rather than merely a rendering library because its ecosystem includes official tools and conventions that support larger applications.

## Enhancing one element vs starting a full app
If you enhance one existing HTML element with Vue, you focus on making a small interactive area update automatically when state changes. If you start a complete Vue application, you typically build a component tree from a root component and let Vue manage the overall reactive rendering across the interface.

pages.title: 02 - Components, Reactivity, and Vue Application Structure
pages.rawNotes:
## Components as the building blocks
Vue interfaces are built by nesting components and connecting them with clear boundaries. A parent component commonly passes data to a child using **props**, and the child communicates back to the parent by **emitting events**. This pattern keeps data flow understandable: props move information downward, and emitted events move user-triggered changes upward.

Props are intended to be read-only from the receiving component’s perspective, which helps prevent accidental state changes in the child. Instead, the child can emit an event when something should change, and the parent can update the source of truth. This is a practical way to structure UI logic so that each component has a focused responsibility.

## Single-File Components and where logic lives
In Vue, a common format is the **Single-File Component** using a `.vue` file. These files typically include a `template` section for the HTML-like markup, a `script` section for component logic, and a `style` section for styling. Even when you do not use this format, the same conceptual pieces still apply: templates describe what to render, and scripts define how state and behavior work.

Here is a minimal example where a parent passes a prop to a child, and the child emits an event when a button is clicked.

```vue
<!-- ChildCounter.vue -->
<template>
  <button @click="emitIncrement">Clicked {{ count }} times</button>
</template>

<script>
export default {
  name: 'ChildCounter',
  props: {
    count: { type: Number, required: true }
  },
  emits: ['increment'],
  methods: {
    emitIncrement() {
      this.$emit('increment')
    }
  }
}
</script>
```

## Reactivity: ref, computed, methods, and watch
Vue components can maintain local reactive state, often using the Composition API with `ref` or `reactive`. **Computed properties** represent derived values that are cached and automatically update when their dependencies change. **Methods** are functions used for actions or reusable component behavior, and **watchers** run logic in response to changes in specified reactive data or computed sources.

A watcher is appropriate when you need side effects after a value changes, such as reacting to a change with additional logic, while a computed value is best when you only need to derive and display updated data.

## Composition API vs Options API
Vue offers both the **Composition API** and the **Options API**, so you may see different organization styles in codebases. The Composition API organizes logic with functions such as `ref`, `reactive`, `computed`, and `watch`, while the Options API organizes behavior under options such as `data`, `methods`, `computed`, and `watch`.

A Vue application typically mounts a root component and renders its component tree, which then handles props, events, and reactive updates throughout the UI.

pages.title: 03 - Vue Ecosystem, Tooling, and React Comparison
pages.rawNotes:
## Vue’s common ecosystem in practice
A modern Vue project is usually assembled from a few well-known tools that work together smoothly. Teams commonly start with the official create-vue scaffolding tool to generate the initial project structure. For building and running the app, Vite is the recommended build tool used in many modern Vue projects. For navigation, Vue Router provides the official routing solution for Vue applications. For shared state across components, Pinia is the recommended state-management library in the Vue ecosystem.

During development, Vue Devtools helps you inspect what is happening inside the app by letting you view component trees, state, events, and performance-related information. If you need server-side rendering, static generation, or full-stack capabilities, Nuxt is a separate Vue-based framework that extends Vue with conventions and features aimed at those needs. Vue supports client-side rendering, and its ecosystem can also support server-side rendering and static generation.

## A minimal Vue project setup
You can create a new Vue project with create-vue, then install dependencies and start a development server. Here is a concrete command sequence that matches that workflow.

```bash
npm create vue@latest
cd <your-project-name>
npm install
npm run dev
```

## Vue vs React: what’s similar and what differs
Vue and React both use components and both support state-driven rendering, so you can think in terms of reusable UI pieces that react to changing data. They also both have ecosystems for routing and state management, which helps teams avoid reinventing common application concerns.

The day-to-day distinction is often syntax and default scope. Vue templates provide an HTML-oriented template system with built-in directives, while React commonly expresses UI structure with JSX. Vue is often described as a progressive framework, while React is commonly described as a JavaScript library centered on UI components.

Neither Vue nor React is universally superior, because the best choice depends on team experience, requirements, ecosystem fit, and project constraints. If you need full-stack features with server-side rendering or static generation, Nuxt can be a strong Vue-centered option for those goals.

bridgeBlocks.title: Vue and React Component Boundaries
bridgeBlocks.body: Vue’s component model maps closely to React’s: both encourage small, reusable components, one-way data flow, and explicit communication between parent and child. React also passes props downward, but child-to-parent communication usually uses callback functions passed as props. Vue Single-File Components typically colocate template, script, and style in a `.vue` file, whereas React commonly colocates JSX and JavaScript or TypeScript, with styles organized separately or included through tooling. quickStart.keyIdea: The Roman Empire was a large, diverse state that grew from the Roman Republic and replaced competitive republican politics with long-term imperial rule centered on emperors.
quickStart.quickSummary:
The Roman Republic was a Mediterranean power governed through elected offices, the Senate, and political competition. The Roman Empire grew directly from that system after conquest, civil wars, and Augustus’s rise in 27 BCE, preserving some republican institutions while concentrating decisive authority in the emperor, supported by armies and provincial administration.

It governed diverse peoples through cities, governors, taxes, laws, citizenship, infrastructure, and military defense, without erasing local customs or religions. The comparison with the Republic breaks down because the Empire was not simply a larger Republic: imperial succession, army influence, and centralized authority reshaped political life. Western rule ended conventionally in 476 CE, while the eastern empire survived until 1453.

pages.title: 01 - From Republic to Empire
pages.rawNotes:
## Big idea
The Roman Empire did not appear suddenly; it grew out of the Roman Republic through conquest, political conflict, and the concentration of power in one ruler.

## From city-state to Mediterranean power
Rome began as a city-state in central Italy and expanded across the Mediterranean world. The Roman Republic relied on elected magistrates, a Senate, assemblies, and written laws, which helped structure political life. As Rome expanded, it gained wealth, enslaved people, taxes, and new territories, and these benefits also intensified competition among powerful leaders.

## The Punic Wars and the stakes of expansion
A major turning point came with the Punic Wars against Carthage, which ended with Roman control of much of the western Mediterranean. With more land and resources, Roman politics became more intense, because leaders could gain influence through military success and control of new revenues. This expansion also increased the number of conflicts that powerful figures could use to build support.

## Late Republic instability
In the late Republic, social conflict, civil wars, and competition among generals became common features of politics. Julius Caesar became dictator for life in 44 BCE, and he was assassinated that same year. Even though his death removed one dominant figure, it did not restore stable republican competition.

## Augustus and the start of imperial rule
Octavian defeated Mark Antony and Cleopatra at Actium in 31 BCE. In 27 BCE, Octavian became Augustus, which is conventionally treated as the beginning of the Roman Empire. Augustus preserved many republican institutions and titles, but real authority was concentrated in the emperor, supported by the army and control of provinces.

## How to think about the change
The Republic and Empire are connected periods, but imperial rule replaced competitive republican politics with dynastic and military power. A helpful way to remember this is that Augustus could keep republican appearances while shifting decisive power away from rival politicians and toward the emperor.

pages.title: 02 - How the Empire Worked
pages.rawNotes:
## Central authority and continuing institutions
The Roman Empire combined one dominant leader with many working parts. The emperor was the central political, military, and religious authority, even though older institutions still existed. The Senate remained important for status, administration, and governing some provinces, so imperial rule did not erase all republican-era structures.

## Provinces, governors, and local governance
To manage distance, the empire was divided into provinces. Governors administered these provinces, collected taxes, judged cases, and maintained order, while imperial authority supervised their work. Cities also mattered because they served as centers of government, commerce, culture, and public buildings. This meant that local communities were not just passive subjects; they were connected to imperial decisions through officials, courts, and civic life.

## The army, infrastructure, and communication
The army defended frontiers and enforced imperial decisions, and it could also influence succession during crises. To support armies and administration, Romans built and maintained roads, ports, bridges, and official communications. These routes helped troops move, merchants trade, and messages travel, which made it easier for the center to coordinate faraway regions.

## Money, law, and citizenship
Taxes and tribute funded government, armies, construction, and the imperial court. Roman law and citizenship connected people to the state, but rights differed by status and location, so legal belonging was not identical for everyone. In 212 CE, Caracalla’s Constitutio Antoniniana granted Roman citizenship to most free inhabitants, strengthening the link between imperial authority and everyday legal identity.

## Roman rule without cultural uniformity
Romanization was uneven across the empire. Cities often adopted Roman institutions and culture, yet local languages, religions, and customs often continued alongside Roman political rule. This helps explain how the empire could integrate diverse peoples while still maintaining Roman authority through provinces, taxation, law, and shared institutions.

### Example: a province in action
Imagine a province where the emperor sets major priorities and appoints key officials. A governor collects taxes, oversees courts, and keeps order, while an army unit protects the frontier and responds to threats. A city council manages local public buildings and commerce, and a taxpayer supports the system through regular payments that help fund administration and defense.

pages.title: 03 - Society, Expansion, Change, and Legacy
pages.rawNotes:
## Roman society: diverse, unequal, and interconnected.
Roman society was not one uniform experience, even though people lived under Roman political rule. At the top were senators, equestrians, and local elites, who held influence and status. Ordinary citizens, freed people, and enslaved people occupied different legal positions, which shaped everyday life and opportunities. Enslaved labor was important in households, agriculture, mining, workshops, and other economic activities, so the empire’s economy depended on unequal social relationships.

## Expansion at its height under Trajan.
Around 117 CE, the empire reached a vast scale under Trajan, covering much of Europe, North Africa, and western Asia. This reach included highly urbanized regions as well as rural, frontier, and desert communities. Because the empire was so large, it created cultural exchange, but it also created frontier pressures and administrative challenges. Managing distant places required ongoing organization, and the empire’s size made stability harder to maintain.

## Change over time: crisis, reorganization, and religion.
During the third century, the empire faced political instability, economic pressures, invasions, and civil wars, which weakened overall stability. In response, Diocletian reorganized imperial government by dividing administrative responsibilities. Later, Constantine supported Christianity after becoming emperor, showing that religious life could shift alongside political power. Christianity began in the Roman world and was initially sometimes persecuted before gaining imperial support.

## Endings and continuities: west in 476, east until 1453.
The western imperial government ended conventionally in 476 CE, but Roman institutions continued elsewhere. The eastern Roman Empire, centered on Constantinople, survived until 1453 and is often called the Byzantine Empire. This means 476 CE is a conventional turning point for the west, not an instant disappearance of Roman political and cultural traditions.

## Quick timeline and social snapshot.
Trajan’s maximum extent around 117 CE was followed by the third-century crisis, then Diocletian’s reorganization, then Constantine’s support for Christianity, then the western government’s conventional end in 476 CE, and finally the eastern empire’s survival until 1453. A social hierarchy example can compare a senator, a citizen farmer, a freed person, and an enslaved worker by focusing on how status affected legal position and economic roles.

## Legacy: what endured.
The empire’s legacy includes law, languages, architecture, Christianity, urban institutions, and ideas of citizenship. Even when political structures changed, these shared institutions and cultural influences helped shape later societies across the former Roman world.

quickStart.keyIdea: Photography is the practice of making deliberate choices about light, focus, composition, and color to record an image with a specific visual purpose.
quickStart.quickSummary:
Lightroom helps organize and refine photographs after capture, while photography fundamentals determine the original image’s brightness, sharpness, motion, depth, color, and visual arrangement. The main exposure choices are aperture, shutter speed, and ISO, each balancing brightness with effects such as background blur, motion freezing, or image noise.

Strong results also depend on observing light, focusing accurately, choosing a supportive composition, and protecting originals through a careful workflow. Lightroom can adjust many aspects non-destructively, but the comparison breaks here: editing cannot reliably restore missed focus, severe motion blur, or permanently clipped detail.

pages.title: 01 - Exposure and the Camera
pages.rawNotes:
## Exposure: what the camera records
Exposure is the amount of light recorded by the camera sensor, and it largely determines whether your photo looks too dark, too bright, or just right. The exposure triangle explains how three controls interact: aperture, shutter speed, and ISO. When you change one side of the triangle, you usually affect both brightness and the look of the image, so it helps to think in trade-offs rather than single “correct” settings.

## Aperture, shutter speed, and ISO
Aperture is the lens opening, expressed with f-numbers such as f/2.8 and f/8. A smaller f-number means a wider opening and generally more light reaching the sensor, and it also tends to create a shallower depth of field. Shutter speed is the length of time the sensor records light, and faster shutter speeds reduce motion blur while slower speeds can show movement or require camera support. ISO changes the camera’s sensitivity or amplification, and higher values usually increase visible noise.

## Checking exposure with meter and histogram
A meter estimates exposure from the scene, but the photographer may need exposure compensation to get the intended result. After capture, a histogram shows the distribution of tones and can help reveal clipped highlights or shadows. For example, a high-key scene often pushes tones toward the brighter side, while a dark scene concentrates tones toward the darker side, and clipping warnings can signal when important detail has been lost.

## RAW vs JPEG and what Lightroom can do
RAW files retain more editable capture data than JPEG files, while JPEGs are processed and compressed in-camera. This matters because Lightroom can refine exposure-related aspects such as highlights and shadows after capture, and it can also adjust white balance. However, detail lost to severe clipping or missed focus may not be recoverable, so it is still important to get the capture as close as possible.

## Examples to connect the concepts
If you compare f/2.8, f/8, and f/16 under similar lighting, the wider aperture (smaller f-number) generally looks brighter and produces more background blur than the narrower aperture. If you photograph a moving subject at 1/30 second versus 1/500 second, the faster shutter speed is more likely to freeze motion and reduce blur. In low light, ISO 100, ISO 800, and ISO 3200 can show how higher ISO enables brighter exposure but typically increases visible noise. For a slightly underexposed RAW image in Lightroom, you can start by increasing exposure, then reduce highlight clipping if needed, and finally adjust shadows to restore tone without creating harsh contrast. A histogram for a high-key scene often shows more data toward the right side, while a dark scene often shows more data toward the left side.

pages.title: 02 - Focus, Light, and Color
pages.rawNotes:
## How Sharpness Happens
Sharpness is not just “having a good camera,” because it depends on accurate focus, sufficient shutter speed, stable technique, and a subject that falls within the chosen depth of field. If the subject is beyond the depth of field, even perfect focus on the wrong plane will look soft. For still subjects, single-shot autofocus is often the best starting point, while continuous autofocus is designed to track movement, though performance can vary by camera and conditions.

Depth of field is the zone that appears acceptably sharp, and it becomes shallower when you use a wider aperture, focus closer, or work in many longer focal-length situations. This means that changing aperture can dramatically change how much of a scene looks sharp, even if exposure stays similar. A practical way to think about it is that wider apertures “spend” sharpness on a thinner slice of space, which can be great for portraits but risky for group photos.

## Light Quality and Direction
Light quality affects contrast, texture, and how shadows look, so it matters as much as exposure. Soft light has gradual transitions and less pronounced shadows, while hard light comes from a smaller, more direct source and creates stronger contrast. The direction and size of the light source also shape modeling, because front light tends to reduce visible texture, while side light emphasizes form and texture.

To apply this, imagine the same subject under different lighting: with side light you should expect more visible texture and clearer shape, while with front light you should expect a smoother look with less texture detail.

## Color: White Balance as Interpretation
White balance adjusts how the camera interprets color so neutral objects appear neutral under different light sources. Different lighting conditions such as daylight, shade, tungsten, and fluorescent can produce different color casts, so the “correct” look depends on the light you are actually shooting. Lightroom supports white-balance presets and temperature and tint controls, and RAW files allow substantial white-balance adjustment after capture, while JPEG correction is more limited.

A helpful habit is to compare the camera’s automatic white balance with a deliberately warm or cool interpretation, because neutrality is not the only valid goal. For example, a window-lit portrait may look natural with a slightly warm setting, while a scene under shade may benefit from correction toward neutral.

## Putting It Together with Examples
For a portrait, choose single-shot autofocus and use a wider aperture to create a shallower depth of field, while for a running subject you would switch to continuous autofocus to track motion. For the same portrait, compare window light, direct noon sun, and a diffuser to see how shadow softness and contrast change. To show depth of field, move closer and change aperture, then observe how the sharp zone shrinks or expands. In Lightroom, compare neutral, warm, and cool white-balance treatments to see how color cast changes the mood. For a focus-check scenario, aim at the eyes with a shallow aperture and confirm that the eye plane is the one that stays sharp.

pages.title: 03 - Composition, Workflow, and Practice
pages.rawNotes:
## Composition: decide what the viewer should notice
Composition is the deliberate arrangement of visual elements within the frame, and it works best when you plan it before you start editing. Start by finding a clear subject and then check the edges for distracting elements that compete for attention. A supportive background and intentional framing improve visual communication, especially when the background does not fight the subject.

Use simple structure to guide your eye, such as the rule of thirds, which places important subjects near a nine-part grid’s intersections or lines. Leading lines can also guide the viewer’s attention through an image, such as a path, a fence line, or the edge of a road. Negative space is relatively unoccupied area that can emphasize a subject or suggest direction, which is useful when you want the subject to feel isolated or purposeful.

One of the most powerful composition tools is changing your camera position, because it alters relationships between foreground, subject, and background. For example, moving lower can emphasize a foreground element, while stepping to the side can separate a subject from a cluttered background. Also remember that focal length changes angle of view and apparent spatial relationships, so it does not simply zoom in every case.

## Workflow: protect originals and refine deliberately
A dependable workflow protects the original file and keeps your edits organized. A basic workflow includes import, backup, selection, adjustment, export, and organization. Import photographs, create a backup, and cull weak or duplicate frames so you only work with images that match your intent.

Then apply global corrections first, and make local adjustments only when needed, because this helps you avoid over-editing. Lightroom’s catalog and non-destructive editing change instructions or previews while preserving the original file, which supports experimentation without losing the capture.

Finally, export settings should match the destination, such as web sharing, printing, or archival storage, so the output fits its purpose. For example, a social-media image typically needs web-friendly sizing, a print needs print-appropriate output, and an archival master should prioritize long-term preservation.

## Examples to practice immediately
Centered composition places the subject in the middle, rule-of-thirds placement shifts the subject toward an intersection or line, and deliberate negative space leaves room around the subject to suggest direction.

If a distracting background object sits behind your subject, change viewpoint by stepping sideways or lowering your position until the object no longer aligns with the subject.

A Lightroom workflow can be: import from the memory card, create a backup, select the best frames, apply global exposure and color adjustments, refine locally if needed, and export a web version while also keeping an organized catalog for later.

For export comparison, choose a social-media export for quick sharing, a print export for physical output, and an archival master export for long-term storage.

If leading lines or repeated shapes pull attention away from the subject, reposition the camera so those lines point toward the subject and the repetition supports the main visual message.

quizQuestions.question: You want a portrait with strong background blur while keeping the subject bright. Which change is most likely to help both goals, assuming lighting and exposure are otherwise managed?
options: Use a wider aperture (smaller f-number)
Use a slower shutter speed (longer exposure)
Increase ISO to the highest value available
quizQuestions.explanation: A wider aperture increases light and typically creates a shallower depth of field, which supports blur.
quizQuestions.skillTested: Applying exposure triangle trade-offs (aperture vs blur/brightness).

quizQuestions.question: A moving subject looks smeared even though the exposure seems okay. What adjustment is most directly aimed at reducing motion blur?
options: Switch to a faster shutter speed
Raise ISO to brighten the image
Change white balance toward warmer tones
quizQuestions.explanation: Faster shutter speeds shorten the recording time and reduce motion blur.
quizQuestions.skillTested: Diagnosing and fixing motion blur using shutter speed.

quizQuestions.question: Your histogram shows important highlight detail is clipped (too far to the bright side). In Lightroom, what sequence best matches the guide’s suggested approach for a slightly underexposed RAW?
options: Increase exposure, then reduce highlight clipping, then adjust shadows
Adjust shadows first, then increase exposure, then change white balance
Reduce highlight clipping first, then lower exposure, then increase ISO
quizQuestions.explanation: The guide suggests increasing exposure first, then reducing highlight clipping, then restoring tone in shadows.
quizQuestions.skillTested: Applying an editing workflow using histogram/clipping cues.

quizQuestions.question: Two photos have similar brightness, but one has noticeably more texture and stronger form. Based on the guide, which lighting setup is the best match for that look?
options: Side light from a larger source
Front light from a smaller, direct source
Side light from a smaller, more direct source
quizQuestions.explanation: Side light emphasizes form and texture, and harder/smaller sources increase contrast.
quizQuestions.skillTested: Comparing light direction and quality effects on texture/contrast.

quizQuestions.question: You’re photographing a runner and need the camera to keep focus as the subject moves. Which autofocus choice best fits the scenario?
options: Single-shot autofocus
Continuous autofocus
Manual focus only, regardless of movement
quizQuestions.explanation: Continuous autofocus is designed to track movement, unlike single-shot.
quizQuestions.skillTested: Selecting focus mode based on subject motion.

quizQuestions.question: A background object keeps visually competing with your subject. Which action most directly follows the guide’s composition strategy?
options: Step sideways or lower your viewpoint to break alignment
Increase ISO to add more noise and reduce distractions
Apply a cooler white-balance preset to shift mood
quizQuestions.explanation: Changing camera position helps separate the subject from a cluttered background by altering alignment.
quizQuestions.skillTested: Applying composition changes by repositioning the camera.

bridgeBlocks.title: From Capture to Lightroom Refinement
bridgeBlocks.body: Photography fundamentals determine what information is captured: focus and depth of field control which areas are sharp, while light direction and color affect contrast, texture, and mood. Lightroom can refine these results after capture with tools such as masking, exposure adjustments, white balance, and color controls. For example, you might brighten a subject or correct a color cast, but you cannot reliably restore detail that was never focused or recorded because of severe blur. A useful workflow is to make capture decisions first, then use Lightroom for organization and controlled refinement.
